1G (Number Theory)

Words: 137 Articles: 1
Paper 1 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 137
1G OurBigBook.com
For an odd prime number p, the Legendre symbol is zero when p∣a, one when a is a nonzero quadratic residue modulo p, and minus one otherwise. The number-theoretic Gauss lemma says that, for p∤a, (a/p)=(−1)r, where r counts those least positive residues of a,2a,…,(p−1)a/2 exceeding p/2.
For a=2, the residues are simply 2,4,…,p−1, so r=(p−1)/2−⌊p/4⌋. Examining the four odd residue classes modulo eight gives
(p2​)=(−1)(p2−1)/8={1−1​p≡1,7(mod8),p≡3,5(mod8).​​
(1)
Now 2m≡−1(modp) and p is odd. The multiplicative order d of 2 divides 2m but not m. Since m is a power of two, every proper divisor of 2m divides m, whence d=2m. Lagrange's theorem for finite groups gives 2m∣p−1. Because m≥4, this implies p≡1(mod8), so the supplementary law just proved gives (2/p)=1. By Euler's criterion, 2(p−1)/2≡1(modp), and consequently 2m∣(p−1)/2. Therefore
p≡1(mod4m)​.
(2)

2F (Topics In Analysis)

Words: 174 Articles: 1
Paper 1 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 174
2F OurBigBook.com
The Liouville approximation theorem states that an irrational algebraic number α of degree d≥2 satisfies ∣α−a/b∣≥Cα​b−d for all integers a and b≥1, for some Cα​>0. The constant is independent of the rational approximation.
The required condition is infinitely many of the coefficients equal one. If only finitely many do, the series is a finite sum of rational numbers. Conversely let α be the sum with infinitely many nonzero terms. Its truncation sN​ has denominator dividing qN​=10N!. For N≥2, its strictly positive tail satisfies
0<α−sN​≤∑j=N+1∞​10−j!<210−(N+1)!=2qN−(N+1)​.
(3)
If α=a/b were rational, the distinct fractions α,sN​ would have distance at least 1/(bqN​), contradicting the tail bound for large N. Thus α is irrational. If it were algebraic of fixed degree d, apply the Liouville approximation theorem to sN​. Even if its reduced denominator is smaller than qN​, the lower bound is at least Cα​qN−d​. The displayed upper bound contradicts this as N→∞. Hence
α is transcendental⟺#{n:ζn​=1}=∞​.
(4)
The coincidence 0!=1! changes only the first rational contribution and has no effect on this criterion.

3G (Coding & Cryptography)

Words: 161 Articles: 1
Paper 1 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 161
3G OurBigBook.com
The ideal observer performs maximum a posteriori decoding: for received word y, it maximizes Pr(X=c∣Y=y), equivalently Pr(X=c)Pr(Y=y∣X=c). Maximum-likelihood decoding maximizes the latter conditional likelihood alone. Minimum-distance decoding minimizes the Hamming distance d(c,y). Ties may be resolved arbitrarily among maximizers.
For independent errors in a binary symmetric channel,
Pr(Y=y∣X=c)=pd(c,y)(1−p)n−d(c,y).
(5)
For 0<p<1/2, its ratio on increasing the distance by one is p/(1−p)<1. Thus maximum-likelihood decoding and minimum-distance decoding select exactly the same codewords. At the allowed endpoint p=0, they agree on a possible observation y∈C; impossible observations have zero likelihood for every codeword, so an arbitrary maximum-likelihood tie rule need not agree with minimum distance. This qualification is needed for the literal assumption p<1/2.
For the specified observation, the Hamming distances from 000 and 111 are two and one. Their likelihoods are 3/64 and 9/64, respectively. After multiplying by the priors, their joint probabilities are 12/320 and 9/320, so their posterior probabilities are 4/7 and 3/7. Therefore
ideal observer: 000,maximum likelihood: 111,minimum distance: 111​.
(6)

a OurBigBook.com
Let a deterministic finite automaton recognizing the regular language have states Q, start state q0​, accepting states F, and transition function δ. Construct a context-free grammar with one nonterminal Aq​ for every state, start symbol Aq0​​, and productions
Aq​→aAδ(q,a)​(q∈Q, a∈Σ),Aq​→ε(q∈F).
(7)
Induction on the length of a word shows that Aq​ derives wAr​ exactly when the automaton reaches r from q after reading w. The terminal production can then end the derivation precisely at an accepting state. Thus the grammar generates exactly the recognized language, proving every regular language is a context-free language. This is actually a right-linear grammar, a special case of a context-free grammar.

b

Words: 164 Articles: 1
4H OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 164
b OurBigBook.com
Treat the fixed letters a1​,…,an​, the empty-language and empty-word symbols, and the punctuation of expressions as a finite token alphabet. In the usual syntax allowing parentheses, union, concatenation, and star, the following context-free grammar generates exactly the syntactically valid regular expressions:
E→∅∣ε∣a1​∣⋯∣an​∣(E)∣E+E∣EE∣E∗.
(8)
Structural induction proves that every generated string is an expression and that every expression has a derivation. Grammar ambiguity does not affect the context-free language assertion.
If the language of these expressions were a regular language, its intersection with the regular token language consisting of some opening parentheses, then a1​, then some closing parentheses would be regular. That intersection is exactly
{(ra1​)r:r≥0}.
(9)
The pumping lemma for regular languages contradicts regularity: a sufficiently long opening-parenthesis prefix forces a pumpable segment wholly within that prefix, and pumping it changes the two parenthesis counts unequally. Hence the expression syntax is context-free but not regular. This conclusion concerns the strings describing expressions, not the languages those expressions denote; it uses the usual concrete syntax with arbitrary nested parentheses.

i OurBigBook.com
The comparison is a nested-model F-test of the three time-by-diet interaction coefficients, with null hypothesis that all are zero. The reduced linear regression model has a common time slope and four diet-specific intercepts; the full model permits four slopes. It has eight fitted coefficients and 579−8=571 residual degrees of freedom.
F=31.589/571(34.381−31.589)/3​≈16.823,F∼F3,571​ under the null​.
(10)
The rounded sums of squares give the displayed approximation; the software reports F=16.824 using unrounded values. The quoted p-value 1.744×10−10 gives overwhelming evidence against equal log-weight growth slopes across diets under the normal linear model assumptions. Thus reject the common-slope hypothesis. Because repeated measurements on the same chicken may be correlated, the exact reference distribution requires independent, homoscedastic Gaussian errors; the displayed ordinary regression output by itself does not establish that assumption.

ii OurBigBook.com
A residual-versus-fitted plot for the untransformed fit places ei​=yi​−y​i​ on the vertical axis and y​i​ on the horizontal axis. A fan-shaped cloud, with larger residual spread at larger fitted weight, suggests heteroscedasticity and approximately multiplicative errors. A logarithmic transformation may stabilize this spread when the conditional standard deviation is roughly proportional to the mean.
One can also use the scale-location plot of ∣ri​∣​ against fitted values, where ri​ is a standardized residual. A systematic rise suggests nonconstant error variance. Neither plot proves that taking logarithms is sufficient: diagnostics of the transformed fit should be checked as well, and dependence between repeated chicken measurements is a separate issue.

ri​=s1−hii​​ei​​,Di​=pri2​​1−hii​hii​​​.
(11)
Thus a contour Di​=d has ri​=±dp(1−hii​)/hii​​. On the actual PDF plot, observation 579 has leverage about 0.084 and standardized residual about −8, lying beyond the D=0.5 contour and below D=1 in influence magnitude, approximately D≃0.7 to 0.8 from the plotted coordinates. τ(t)=⎩⎨⎧​2αD​(e2αt−1)Dt​α=0,α=0.​​

Then τ′=De2αt>0 and the porous medium equation is Rτ​=(R2Rx​)x​. Its total mass is conserved when the flux vanishes at infinity. For the mass-preserving similarity solution, direct differentiation gives
Rτ​=−41​τ−5/4(F+ξF′),(R2Rx​)x​=τ−5/4(F2F′)′,∫R​Fdξ=N0​.

There is an important convention issue in the printed statement. The ordinary Cauchy principal value exists only for n=1. Closing the Fourier contour in the lower half-plane, with a small indentation above the real-axis pole, gives
PV∫R​xe−ix​dx=−iπ​.
(15)
Equivalently, the odd cosine contribution cancels and the Dirichlet integral ∫0∞​sinx/xdx=π/2 supplies the imaginary part.
For n≥2, the paired integrand near zero is 2cosx/xn if n is even and −2isinx/xn if n is odd. Its leading even power is nonintegrable: x−n in the first case and x1−n in the second. Thus the ordinary principal value diverges for every n>1.
If the intended convention is the Hadamard finite-part integral, define it consistently by distributional differentiation,
Pfxn1​=(n−1)!(−1)n−1​dxn−1dn−1​PVx1​.
(16)
Integration by parts in this distributional pairing, or regularized Fourier transformation, then gives
Pf∫R​xne−ix​dx=(n−1)!π(−i)n​​.
(17)
The distinction is essential: subtracting the divergent local Taylor terms supplies a finite part, but symmetric exclusion alone does not.

Assume the holonomic constraints have linearly independent gradients, so their common level set is locally a smooth constraint manifold parametrized by q1​,…,qn​. The multiplier form of the Euler-Lagrange equations is
dtd​Lx˙A​​−LxA​​=∑α​λα​∂A​fα​.
(18)
At fixed time ∑A​∂A​fα​∂i​xA​=0. The chain rule for the reduced Lagrangian gives
dtd​Lq˙​i​​−Lqi​​=∑A​(dtd​Lx˙A​​−LxA​​)∂i​xA​=0.
(19)
Conversely, if these reduced equations hold, the Cartesian Euler-Lagrange residual annihilates every tangent direction. Linear independence of the constraint gradients implies that it is a linear combination of those gradients, giving the required Lagrange multipliers. This proves the local equivalence, including time-dependent constraints; singular constraints would need separate analysis.
For the bead, y˙​=f′(x)x˙, so
L=21​(1+f′(x)2)x˙2​,(1+f′2)x¨+f′f′′x˙2=0.
(20)
The autonomous conservation of energy gives E=21​(1+f′2)x˙2. If E>0, the motion has a fixed sign s=sgnx˙ and
t=t∗​+2E​s​∫x∗​x​1+f′(u)2​du​.
(21)
The integral is the signed arc length divided by the constant speed, and is locally invertible. The special solution E=0 is a stationary bead, for which writing time as a function of its unchanging position is not meaningful.

9C (Cosmology)

Words: 137 Articles: 1
Paper 1 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 137
9C OurBigBook.com
For comoving galaxies their relative comoving vector χ is constant, and the physical displacement is r(t)=a(t)χ, where a is the scale factor. Differentiating gives the Hubble law
v=Hr,H=aa˙​​.
(22)
Peculiar velocity relative to this comoving frame is excluded in this relation.
Transport a wave crest between neighbouring comoving observers separated by a small physical distance dℓ. Their recession speed is Hdℓ, while the light travel time is dt=dℓ/c to first order. The local Doppler shift therefore changes its wavelength by dλ/λ=Hdt. Multiplying these infinitesimal shifts along the ray, or integrating their logarithms, yields
logλe​λ0​​=∫te​t0​​H(t)dt=loga(te​)a(t0​)​,1+z=a(te​)a(t0​)​​.
(23)
The use of the local first-order Doppler law is exact in the limit of infinitesimal steps: the accumulated second-order errors tend to zero. A single special-relativistic recession velocity assigned to widely separated galaxies would not justify this cosmological redshift relation.

i OurBigBook.com
A linear code of length n and rank k is a k-dimensional linear subspace of F2n​. The Hamming weight of a vector counts its nonzero coordinates. Thus the sum of the coefficients of the weight enumerator is the number of codewords:
WC​(1,1)=2k​.
(24)
Since the zero vector is the unique word of weight zero, WC​(0,1)=1. Symmetry of the enumerator therefore implies WC​(1,0)=1. Conversely WC​(1,0)=1 means that the all-one vector 1 belongs to C. Translation x↦x+1 is then a bijection of C which replaces weight j by n−j, proving the polynomial symmetry. For length zero the same conclusion holds with the unique empty vector.
The dual code is C⊥={y:x⋅y=0 for every x∈C}, using the standard bilinear form over F2​. If y∈C⊥, each summand of the character sum equals one. Otherwise choose x0​∈C with x0​⋅y=1; replacing x by x+x0​ permutes the summands and reverses their sign. The sum equals its own negative and must be zero. Consequently
x∈C∑​(−1)x⋅y=2k1{y∈C⊥}​​.
(25)
This is character orthogonality for the additive group of the code.

ii OurBigBook.com
For any vector y∈F2n​, use its Hamming weight w(y)=#{j:yj​=1}. The stated product identity also follows directly by summing each coordinate independently:
∑y​uw(y)(−1)x⋅y=∏j=1n​(1+(−1)xj​u)=(1−u)w(x)(1+u)n−w(x).
(26)
For t=0, interchange the two finite sums with u=s/t. Character orthogonality evaluates the inner sum over codewords, whereas the product identity evaluates the sum over all binary vectors. Thus
2k∑y∈C⊥​(s/t)w(y)=∑x∈C​(1−s/t)w(x)(1+s/t)n−w(x).
(27)
Multiply by tn to obtain the MacWilliams identity in the paper's weight-enumerator convention:
WC⊥​(s,t)=2−kWC​(t−s,t+s)​.
(28)
Both sides are polynomials, so equality for t=0 extends to t=0 as well; the intermediate quotient is not a restriction on the final identity.

a

11H OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 194
a OurBigBook.com
A deterministic finite automaton is described by finite state and alphabet label lists, one initial state label, an accepting-state bit mask, and a finite transition table. Keep each label in increasing order and list transitions lexicographically by the actual state and alphabet labels. This retains arbitrary finite subsets of the permitted labels, rather than assuming they are consecutive.
The prime-exponent encoding of a finite list gives an explicit Gödel encoding for a list (a0​,…,ar−1​) of nonnegative integers:
code(a0​,…,ar−1​)=2r∏j=0r−1​pj+2aj​+1​,
(29)
where pi​ is the ith prime number. Encode the descriptor as a list beginning with the numbers of states and alphabet symbols, followed by their sorted labels, the start label, the accepting mask, and all transition destinations. The lengths are then known during decoding.
Unique prime factorization recovers the list and hence the automaton. Reject an integer if the prescribed prime exponents are missing, additional primes occur, the list lengths disagree, state or alphabet labels repeat, the initial state or a transition target is absent, or the mask is out of range. These are effective finite checks. Thus every automaton has an integer code, valid codes are decidable, and the transition system of a coded automaton is computable. Invalid integers may be excluded explicitly or assigned a fixed empty-language automaton.

b

Words: 196 Articles: 1
11H OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 196
b OurBigBook.com
From the decoded deterministic finite automaton, retain only productive states: those reachable from the initial state and from which an accepting state is reachable. Both sets are computable by finite graph search. Its regular language is infinite precisely when this productive directed graph contains a directed cycle.
Indeed, a cycle on a route from the start to acceptance can be repeated arbitrarily often, giving accepted words of different lengths. Conversely an accepted path of length at least the number of productive states repeats one such state and gives a productive cycle. Therefore absence of cycles bounds every accepted length strictly below that number. Cycle detection is a finite algorithm, proving that finiteness of the accepted language is decidable.
When it is finite, enumerate every word of length less than the number of states and simulate acceptance, then count the accepted words. This includes the empty word. Alternatively use dynamic programming in the productive acyclic graph:
N(q)=1{q accepting}​+∑a:δ(q,a) productive​N(δ(q,a)).
(30)
Distinct alphabet symbols count distinct words even when their transitions share a destination. The result is N(q0​), or zero if the start state is not productive. Validity of the encoding is checked first, so the set of valid finite-language codes is recursive set.

Under the binomial distribution model's assumption of independent games with a common win probability p, the probability of winning a match is
h(p)=∑j=611​(j11​)pj(1−p)11−j.
(31)
This is also the cumulative distribution function F6,6​(p) of a Beta distribution with parameters (6,6): differentiation of the binomial tail gives h′(p)=11!p5(1−p)5/(5!)2, and h(0)=0. In particular h is strictly increasing on (0,1) and maps [0,1] bijectively onto itself.
The new match probability is Pab​=h(Pab​), while the desired linear predictor remains the game-level log odds. Therefore the link function is
g(u)=log1−F6,6−1​(u)F6,6−1​(u)​​,0<u<1.
(32)
Its endpoint values are −∞ and +∞. This is not the ordinary match-level log odds link: it first recovers the underlying game probability. Symmetry of the binomial tail gives h(1−p)=1−h(p), hence g(1−u)=−g(u), as required by swapping the players. Dependence or varying game probabilities within a match would invalidate the stated binomial-tail conversion.

For Res>1, expand (et−1)−1=∑n≥1​e−nt. Absolute integrability, bounded near zero by a constant times tRes−2, permits termwise integration. The Gamma function integral then gives
∫0∞​et−1ts−1​dt=∑n≥1​n−sΓ(s),ζR​(s)=Γ(s)1​∫0∞​et−1ts−1​dt​.
(33)
Specify the Hankel contour to run from the negative real axis below the cut towards zero, circle zero counterclockwise with fixed radius 0<r<2π, and return above the cut. Take −π<argt<π. The circle excludes every nonzero pole 2πiZ of the denominator. For Res>1 its radius can shrink to zero, and the lower and upper rays give respectively −e−iπsΓ(s)ζR​(s) and eiπsΓ(s)ζR​(s). By the Gamma reflection formula,
I(s)=πΓ(1−s)Γ(s)sinπs​ζR​(s)=ζR​(s)
(34)
away from integer s in that half-plane, with limiting equality at the removable points.
With the circle radius kept fixed, the contour integral is an entire function of s: the rays decay exponentially and converge locally uniformly, and the circular part stays away from zero. Multiplication by Γ(1−s) is analytic for Res<1 and meromorphic globally. The apparent singularities at positive integers s≥2 are removable because the integral vanishes there and it already agrees with the original analytic zeta function nearby. Only s=1 remains a simple pole. Thus this constructs the meromorphic continuation to the whole plane and an analytic continuation on C∖{1}. Keeping the circular segment is essential when the integral is not locally integrable at zero.
At s=−1 the two rays cancel, since t−2 is single-valued. The Laurent expansion
e−t−11​=−t1​−21​−12t​+O(t3)
(35)
shows that the residue of t−2/(e−t−1) is −1/12. Since Γ(2)=1, the residue theorem gives
ζR​(−1)=−121​​.

15H (Logic and Set Theory)

Words: 264 Articles: 1
Paper 1 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 264
15H OurBigBook.com
The completeness theorem for propositional logic, together with soundness, states S⊢φ if and only if S⊨φ. In particular, an inconsistent set of formulae has a finite formal proof of contradiction. Such a proof uses only finitely many assumptions, yielding the propositional compactness theorem: if every finite subset of S is satisfiable, then S is satisfiable.
The decidability theorem for propositional logic concerns theoremhood of a formula, or entailment from a finite list of premises. Formulae involve finitely many variables, so their valuations can be tested by a finite truth table; completeness identifies semantic validity with provability. Equivalently, dovetail effective proof enumeration with the finite search for a countervaluation: completeness ensures that one succeeds. This is not a decidability claim for consequences of an arbitrary noncomputable infinite theory.
An infinite collection of distinct tautologies is a finitary set of formulae, since its deductive closure equals that of the empty set. By contrast, the set of independent variables {pi​:i≥1} is not finitary. If a finite set T had the same closure, it would mention only finitely many variables. It is satisfiable because it is a consequence of the all-true model of the pi​; changing an unmentioned pj​ to false preserves T and contradicts T⊨pj​.
Under the final hypothesis, A∪B has no model. The propositional compactness theorem gives finite A′⊂A, B′⊂B with A′∪B′ inconsistent. Any valuation satisfying A′ cannot satisfy B, because it would then satisfy B′; by the exactly-one hypothesis it must satisfy A. The reverse implication holds by inclusion. Thus A and A′ have identical models, and similarly B and B′. Completeness gives identical deductive closures, proving
A and B are finitary​.
(41)

Let v1​⋯vr​ be a longest path in the finite simple graph. Every neighbour of either endpoint lies on it. Among indices 1≤i<r, consider those with edges v1​vi+1​ and those with edges vi​vr​. Their cardinalities are the endpoint degrees, whose sum is at least n≥r, exceeding the r−1 available indices. They intersect, producing the cycle
v1​v2​⋯vi​vr​vr−1​⋯vi+1​v1​.
(42)
Every connected component has at least δ(G)+1>n/2 vertices, so the graph is connected. If r<n, an edge joins a vertex outside this cycle to it, and breaking the cycle there gives a longer path, a contradiction. Hence r=n and this is a Hamilton cycle, proving Dirac theorem.
The complete graph K4​ is planar, has chromatic number four and a Hamilton cycle. Adding one leaf attached to one of its vertices preserves planarity and chromatic number four but prevents a Hamilton cycle, since a leaf has degree one.
For the last claim, the given plane embedding has all vertices on the outer cycle. Add noncrossing diagonals until its polygonal interior is triangulated. A triangulated polygon has a vertex incident with only its two boundary neighbours: for example the dual graph of its triangles is a tree and a leaf triangle supplies an ear. Remove this vertex. Inductively three-colour the smaller triangulated polygon, starting with a triangle. The removed vertex's neighbours are adjacent and have different colours, so it can receive the third. Restriction to the original graph gives
χ(G)≤3​.
(43)
This uses the specified embedding, not the false assertion that every planar Hamiltonian graph is three-colourable; K4​ is already a counterexample to that broader assertion.

A splitting field of a nonzero polynomial f over K is an extension in which f splits into linear factors and which is generated over K by all its roots. For a constant nonzero polynomial the splitting field is K; the zero polynomial does not have a root-generated splitting field in this standard definition.
Given two splitting fields L,L′, enumerate the roots generating L and extend a K-embedding one root at a time. If an embedding is defined on K(α1​,…,αj​), the minimal polynomial of the next root divides f over that field. Its image under the embedding therefore divides f over the corresponding subfield of L′, and has a root in L′. The quotient construction K(α)≅K[t]/(mα​) extends the embedding to that root. The polynomial need not be a separable polynomial.
At the end this gives a K-embedding L→L′. It sends the distinct roots of f injectively to its roots, hence permutes the finite set of distinct roots and contains every root in its image. Since these generate L′, the embedding is onto. Thus the splitting field is unique up to a (K)-isomorphism.

f(t)≡(t−1)(t3+t2+t−2)(mod5),f(t)≡(t+2)(t+3)(t2+2t−2)(mod7).

The cubic modulo five has no root in F5​, hence is irreducible. The quadratic modulo seven has discriminant five, a nonsquare there. The Frobenius cycle type theorem therefore supplies a three-cycle and a transposition in the group.
Transitivity implies that its order is divisible by four, and the three-cycle implies divisibility by three. Its order divides 24, so it is 12 or 24. The only subgroup of index two in S4​ is A4​: an index-two subgroup is the kernel of a group homomorphism of a nontrivial homomorphism to C2​, and all transpositions are conjugate and generate S4​, forcing this homomorphism to be the sign. The exhibited transposition excludes A4​. Hence
Gal(t4+2t+2/Q)≅S4​​.

Modulo three, the quintic has no linear factor: its value is −1 at every element of F3​. The monic irreducible quadratics over this field are t2+1, t2+t+2 and t2+2t+2. Division leaves respectively −1, t−1 and t−1, all nonzero. A reducible quintic has a factor of degree at most two, so it is irreducible modulo three and therefore over Q. Its Galois group is transitive on five roots.
Modulo two its squarefree factorization is
t5−t−1≡(t2+t+1)(t3+t2+1).
(46)
Both factors are irreducible, so the Frobenius cycle type theorem gives an element that is a disjoint transposition times a three-cycle. Cubing it gives a transposition.
The prime-degree transposition criterion can be proved here: a transitive subgroup of prime degree containing a transposition is the whole symmetric group. Construct a graph on the five roots whose edges are the pairs swapped by all conjugates of this transposition. The group acts transitively on vertices and permutes connected components, so all component sizes are equal and divide five. An edge rules out size one; the graph is connected. Edge transpositions of any connected graph generate the full symmetric group, for instance by transporting swaps along a spanning tree. All belong to the Galois group, proving
Gal(t5−t−1/Q)≅S5​​.
(47)
The prime-degree condition is essential to the short transposition argument.

Consider the singularity of the injective entire function f at infinity. If removable, it is bounded outside a disk and therefore bounded globally; Liouville theorem makes it constant, a contradiction. If essential, the Casorati-Weierstrass theorem says its values outside every large disk are dense. Choose a small neighbourhood U of a finite point; the open mapping theorem puts a nonempty open disk inside f(U). A point outside a disk containing U would map into that open disk, duplicating a value already attained in U. This contradicts injectivity. Thus infinity is a pole, so f is a polynomial. If its degree were greater than one, its derivative would have a root; the local power-series form at that point has local degree at least two and cannot be injective. Hence
f(z)=az+b,a=0​.

For a nonconstant holomorphic map of connected compact Riemann surfaces of degree d, the Riemann-Hurwitz formula is
2gR​−2=d(2gS​−2)+∑p∈R​(ep​−1),

where gR​,gS​ are genera and ep​ is the local mapping degree, the multiplicity in the target fibre. There are finitely many points with ep​>1.
For a degree-two sphere map, the formula gives total ramification two. Since ep​≤2, there are exactly two distinct ramification points, each of local degree two. Their images are distinct, since a fibre has total multiplicity two. Choose a Möbius transformation T taking 0,∞ to these domain points and S0​ taking their images to 0,∞. The resulting rational map has its only zero at zero of order two and its only pole at infinity of order two, hence is cz2 with c=0. Replace S0​ by S(z)=c−1S0​(z), obtaining
S∘f∘T(z)=z2​.

a OurBigBook.com
A morphism of algebraic varieties is a map regular in local affine coordinates: for each point of the source, choose affine charts containing it and its image, and require each target coordinate to pull back locally to a quotient of polynomials with a denominator nonzero at that point. The map is continuous in the Zariski topology and pulls back regular functions on every target open set to regular functions on its inverse image.
Equivalently, one can take Zariski continuity and this local regular-function pullback property as the definition. In particular, a morphism between affine varieties is specified by globally regular coordinate functions, with values satisfying the defining equations of the target. Being an arbitrary set-theoretic function, or being merely Zariski continuous, is not sufficient.

On a neighbourhood of every point it has the form a/b, where a,b∈A and b does not vanish at that point. J={h∈A:hf∈A}.

A time-homogeneous continuous-time Markov chain on a countable state space is a stochastic process with the Markov property: conditional on the current state, the law of its future depends on neither its past nor the current time. In the usual conservative, nonexplosive setting its sample paths are right-continuous step functions. Its Q-matrix Q=(qij​) has qij​≥0 for j=i, qi​=−qii​=∑j=i​qij​<∞, and infinitesimal transition probabilities Pi​(X(h)=j)=qij​h+o(h) for j=i.
On entering i, the holding time has distribution Exp(qi​); independently, the next state is j with probability qij​/qi​. The successive states form the jump chain, whose transition probabilities are
pij​=qij​/qi​(j=i),pii​=0(qi​>0)​.
(98)
If qi​=0, the state is absorbing, its holding time is infinite, and the jump-chain convention is pii​=1. Nonexplosion ensures this construction defines the process for all finite times rather than accumulating infinitely many jumps in finite time.

For β=1 the fixed points are the origin, four axis points (±1,0),(0,±1), and four diagonal points (±s,±s) with independent signs and s=(1+β)−1/2. The hypothesis β>−1 ensures that s is real. The Jacobian matrix has diagonal entries −1+3x2+βy2, −1+βx2+3y2 and off-diagonal entries 2βxy.
At the origin both eigenvalues are −1, so it is a stable node. At each axis point the eigenvalues are 2,β−1. At each diagonal point they are 2,2(1−β)/(1+β), along the radial and transverse diagonal directions respectively. Thus

For β=1/2 the axis saddle points have stable directions transverse to their axes and unstable directions along them; the diagonal points are unstable nodes. For β=2 these roles switch: the diagonal saddle points have stable transverse directions and unstable radial directions, and the axis points are unstable nodes. Their stable manifolds separate trajectories attracted to the origin from outward-escaping trajectories. Symmetry gives the other quadrants.
For β=1, the entire unit circle consists of equilibria. In polar coordinates r˙=r(r2−1) and θ˙=0: every ray inside the circle moves toward the origin, and every ray outside moves outward. The circle has neutral tangential and unstable radial directions; its points are not isolated saddle points or unstable nodes.

(121)
A first integral F obeys dF/dt={F,H}=0. Consequently [VF​,VH​]=0, and the local flows commute. The time-independent transformation generated by VF​, with t unchanged, therefore maps integral curves of a vector field for VH​ to integral curves of a vector field: it is a Lie point symmetry.
Conversely, such a time-independent symmetry gives [VF​,VH​]=0, hence V{F,H}​=0. Nondegeneracy of J makes {F,H} constant on each connected component. At a fixed point x0​, J∇H(x0​)=0 implies ∇H(x0​)=0, so that constant is zero on its component. Thus the converse holds on a connected phase space containing a fixed point, or on each component that contains one.
The printed global converse needs this connectedness convention: a fixed point on one component does not control the constants on other components. For example take one component with H=(q2+p2)/2, F=0, and another with H=p, F=q. The Hamiltonian vector fields commute everywhere and there is a fixed point on the first component, but F is not a first integral on the second. Even on a connected space the fixed-point condition matters: H=p, F=q commute but F˙=1.

Invert the operator definitions to obtain a=mω/(2ℏ)​x^+ip^​/2ℏmω​ and the adjoint formula for a†. The canonical commutation relation yields [a,a†]=1, with [a,a]=[a†,a†]=0. Substitution gives
H=ℏω(a†a+21​)​.

Write N=a†a≥0. Since [N,a]=−a and [N,a†]=a†, these are lowering and raising operators. Applying a to a ground state would lower its energy unless it vanishes, so a∣0⟩=0. From the normalized unique ground state construct
∣n⟩=n!​(a†)n​∣0⟩,En​=ℏω(n+21​),n=0,1,…​.
(123)
The commutator gives the factorial normalization and a∣n⟩=n​∣n−1⟩. For any energy eigenstate, repeated lowering cannot pass below N=0; positivity of each lowered norm forces its N eigenvalue to be a nonnegative integer and lowering eventually reaches the ground state. Its uniqueness then yields the entire eigenstate ladder. The usual oscillator on the real line has discrete complete spectrum because its potential is confining, so these states span its Hilbert space.
For the perturbation λW with W=ℏω(a2+a†2), nondegenerate time-independent perturbation theory gives En′​=En​+λWnn​+λ2∑m=n​∣Wmn​∣2/(En​−Em​)+O(λ3). The first-order term vanishes. Only m=n−2,n+2 contribute, with squared matrix elements (ℏω)2n(n−1) and (ℏω)2(n+1)(n+2) respectively. Thus
En′​=ℏω(n+21​)−λ2ℏω(2n+1)+O(λ3)​.
(124)
The absent downward transition for n=0,1 is automatically represented by n(n−1)=0. Direct substitution also gives
H′=2m1−2λ​p^​2+2mω2(1+2λ)​x^2.
(125)
For ∣λ∣<1/2 this is another oscillator with mass m′=m/(1−2λ) and frequency ω′=ω1−4λ2​. Therefore
En′​=ℏω1−4λ2​(n+21​)​.
(126)
Its expansion is En​[1−2λ2+O(λ4)], agreeing with the perturbative result and sharpening its remainder. At the excluded endpoints confinement is lost; beyond them the quadratic Hamiltonian is not bounded below.

33C OurBigBook.com
The normalized Bloch states ∣k⟩=N−1/2∑n=1N​eikna∣n⟩ satisfy periodicity when k=2πj/(Na). Acting with the hopping terms shifts the coefficients by one site, giving
H∣k⟩=(E0​−2Jcoska)∣k⟩​.
(127)
The first Brillouin zone is a fundamental cell of reciprocal space, for example [−π/a,π/a); wavevectors differing by 2π/a label the same state. It contains exactly N distinct allowed wavevectors and hence N orbital states. The written Hamiltonian has no spin index; if electron spin degeneracy is included there are 2N states.
For a narrow wave packet, group velocity and band-curvature effective mass are
v(k)=ℏ2Ja​sinka,m∗(k)=2Ja2coskaℏ2​​.
(128)
For the usual J>0, the mass is negative in the outer half of the zone, π/(2a)<∣k∣≤π/a, taking one endpoint representative. At ∣k∣=π/(2a) the inverse mass vanishes and the mass diverges. For arbitrary nonzero J, the sign criterion is Jcoska<0; J=0 is a flat band.
For electron charge −e with e>0 in a constant electric field E, the single-band semiclassical equations are ℏk˙=−eE, x˙=v(k). Thus k(t)=k0​−eEt/ℏ, and for E=0,
x(t)−x0​=eE2J​[cos(k0​a−ℏeEa​t)−cosk0​a]​.
(129)
These are Bloch oscillations of period 2πℏ/(∣eE∣a). The zero-field limit is x−x0​=v(k0​)t. This assumes a narrow packet and neglects scattering and interband transitions.
For many electrons obeying the Pauli exclusion principle, a partially filled band has available nearby states and can carry current under a displaced occupation distribution: it describes a metal within band theory. A completely filled band has cancelling velocities over the zone, so its current is zero; if separated from empty higher bands by a nonzero gap, it describes an insulator at sufficiently low temperature and weak electric field. With spin degeneracy this isolated band is filled at two electrons per site. The single-electron Hamiltonian alone does not specify the filling or a gap to a next band, so those extra physical assumptions are required for classifying a material.

The microcanonical ensemble assigns equal probability to accessible quantum states in a narrow energy shell of an isolated system with fixed energy, particle number and external parameters. To derive the canonical ensemble, put a small system in weak thermal contact with a much larger isolated bath. If the small-system state has energy Ei​, its probability is proportional to the number Ωb​(Etotal​−Ei​) of bath states. Expanding the bath entropy gives Sb​(Etotal​−Ei​)=Sb​(Etotal​)−Ei​/T+⋯, since ∂Sb​/∂E=1/T. Negligible interaction energy and an effectively constant bath temperature therefore give pi​=e−Ei​/(kB​T)/Z. The microcanonical ensemble suits an isolated fixed-energy system; the canonical ensemble suits a system exchanging energy with a thermostat at fixed temperature, with particle number still fixed.
For one atom, summing the finite geometric series over m=−J,…,J gives the partition function
Z1​=m=−J∑J​exm=sinh(x/2)sinh((J+1/2)x)​,x=kB​TμB​B​​.
(130)
At x=0 the ratio is understood by continuity as 2J+1. Logarithmic differentiation gives the mean magnetic dipole moment
⟨μz​⟩=μB​[(J+21​)coth((J+21​)x)−21​coth(x/2)]​.
(131)
This is odd in x, has small-x expansion μB​J(J+1)x/3+O(x3), and saturates at ±JμB​. The requested common graph is plotted in units of μB​: its ordinate is ⟨μz​⟩/(JμB​), so multiplication by μB​ gives ⟨μz​⟩/J. The normalized slopes at zero are (J+1)/3 and the limits are ±1.
The magnetic susceptibility is
χ=kB​TNμB2​​[41​csch2(x/2)−(J+21​)2csch2((J+21​)x)]​.
(132)
Equivalently it is NμB2​Var(m)/(kB​T)≥0. For kB​T≫μB​∣B∣, the apparent singular terms cancel, yielding Curie law
χ∼3kB​TNμB2​J(J+1)​​.
(133)
For fixed nonzero B, T→0 and integer J≥1, the first excited magnetic level is separated from the aligned ground state by μB​∣B∣. Its exponentially small occupation gives
χ∼kB​TNμB2​​e−μB​∣B∣/(kB​T)⟶0​.
(134)
The moments are saturated, so changing the magnetic field hardly changes their alignment. This is a fixed-nonzero-field low-temperature limit. At exactly B=0, differentiating first gives the Curie expression for every T>0, which diverges as T→0; the two limits do not commute in this noninteracting model. For J=0 both moment and susceptibility vanish identically.

Use a Lorentz boost along positive x with v=E/B. Since E<cB, its dimensionless speed β=E/(cB) is less than one. The given transformation of the electric field and magnetic field yields Ey′​=γ(β)(E−vB)=0 and
β=cBE​,B′=B1−β2​=B2−E2/c2​​.
(135)
All other electric components vanish. In this frame a magnetic field does no work, so the particle's speed u<c and Lorentz factor γu​=(1−u2/c2)−1/2 are constant. In proper time, the Lorentz force equations are d(γu​ux′​)/dτ=(qB′/m)γu​uy′​ and d(γu​uy′​)/dτ=−(qB′/m)γu​ux′​. Thus, choosing the phase and origin,
ct′=γu​cτ,x′=ωγu​u​sinωτ,y′=ωγu​u​cosωτ,ω=mqB′​​.
(136)
This is the signed proper-time cyclotron frequency; the frequency with respect to t′ is ω/γu​. The inverse Lorentz boost gives
ctxy​=γu​γ(β)(cτ+ωβu​sinωτ),=γu​γ(β)(βcτ+ωu​sinωτ),=ωγu​u​cosωτ.​​
(137)
In particular the average drift speed is βc=E/B along E×B.
For u>0, q=0, set s=ωτ and d=βc/u. The dimensionless spatial curve is
x=γ(β)(ds+sins),y​=coss​.
(138)
The drift between successive cycles is 2πγ(β)d. When 2πβ≪u/c, this is small compared with the oscillation size: the curve consists of nearly closed loops with slow rightward drift. When 2πβ≫u/c, the longitudinal drift is large, producing a progressing oscillatory curve. More precisely dx/ds=γ(β)(d+coss): loops occur for d<1, cusps at d=1, and monotone progression for d>1. The stated large-drift inequality compares the drift over a full cycle, so an example of that regime with d>1 is shown; that comparison alone does not replace the exact loop criterion.
Reversing q reverses the cyclotron orientation; the drift remains along positive x. If u=0 the trajectory is pure straight drift and the dimensionless coordinates are undefined. If q=0 the particle is inertial and the displayed 1/ω parametrization must be replaced by its inertial limit.

Put h(r)=1−μ/r2. For the equatorial geodesic, the geodesic Lagrangian is L=21​[−ht˙2+h−1r˙2+r2ϕ˙​2], where dots denote derivatives with respect to the affine parameter. The cyclic coordinates t,ϕ give constants pt​=−ht˙=−E and pϕ​=r2ϕ˙​=L. A third constant is the tangent norm gab​x˙ax˙b=−κ, preserved by the geodesic equation and metric compatibility. For a timelike geodesic rescale the affine parameter to proper time so κ=1; for a null geodesic κ=0.
Substitute t˙=E/h, ϕ˙​=L/r2 into the norm identity and multiply by h. It gives the effective potential equation
21​r˙2+V(r)=21​E2,V(r)=21​(1−r2μ​)(κ+r2L2​)​.
(139)
Outside the horizon r=μ​, its derivative is V′=−(L2−κμ)/r3+2μL2/r5. A nontrivial circular null geodesic requires L=0, giving
rnull​=2μ​,V′′(rnull​)=−2μ2L2​<0​.
(140)
For a circular timelike geodesic,
rtime2​=L2−μ2μL2​,L2>μ​.
(141)
At it V′′=−4μL2/r6<0, and its radius exceeds 2μ​. If L2≤μ no finite circular timelike radius exists. Thus all finite circular null and timelike orbits in this five-dimensional exterior are radially unstable. The energy of a circular orbit is fixed by E2=2V(r), not independently arbitrary.
For comparison, with four-dimensional Schwarzschild horizon radius rs​, the photon circle is at 3rs​/2 and is unstable. Circular timelike orbits exist for r>3rs​/2; they are unstable below 3rs​, marginal at 3rs​ and stable above 3rs​. The five-dimensional potential has no corresponding stable outer circular timelike branch.

The unit normal pointing out of the fluid at its lower boundary is −ey​. Since impermeability gives v(x,0)=0, also vx​(x,0)=0, and the tangential viscous traction exerted on the fluid is tx​=−μuy​(x,0). The cilia do positive work at rate tx​u=ρP, so
uuy​​y=0​=−ρP/μ=−P/ν​.
(142)
For positive downstream velocity this requires uy​<0, as expected when the wall-driven flow slows away from the cilia. The wall velocity is not prescribed independently; the driving condition prescribes power.
In a laminar boundary layer, momentum diffuses over a thickness δ during the downstream advection time x/U, giving δ2∼νx/U. The wall power condition gives U2/δ∼P/ν. With these balances the downstream Reynolds number grows and δ/x∝x−3/5 tends to zero. This explains the thin layer for large x within the laminar approximation. Pressure is uniform across it and has no imposed streamwise gradient because the outer fluid is at rest. The two-dimensional boundary-layer equations are
uux​+vuy​=νuyy​,ux​+vy​=0.
(143)
Choose the scales to satisfy the balances exactly:
U(x)=(νP2x​)1/5,δ(x)=(Pν3x2​)1/5​.
(144)
The stream function ψ=Uδf(η), η=y/δ, enforces continuity equation and gives
u=Uf′,v=5xUδ​(2ηf′−3f),ux​=5xU​(f′−2ηf′′).
(145)
Thus the advective term is U2[51​f′2−53​ff′′]/x, while νuyy​=νUf′′′/δ2=U2f′′′/x. Hence
f′′′=51​f′2−53​ff′′​.
(146)
Impermeability, imposed wall power and matching to resting outer fluid give
f(0)=0,f′(0)f′′(0)=−1,f′(η)→0(η→∞)​.
(147)
A regular decaying profile also has f′′→0 and finite positive f∞​; no arbitrary additional wall value for f′ should be imposed.
The volume flux per unit span is Q=∫0∞​udy=Uδf∞​∝x3/5, so continuity equation gives v∞​=−dQ/dx<0: outer fluid is entrained toward the wall. In the physical positive decaying similarity profile, f′>0 and f′′<0. To justify monotonicity, f′′(0)<0 by the power condition; if f′′ first crossed zero with f′>0, the equation would give f′′′=f′2/5>0, after which f′′>0 cannot cross back and f′ could not decay to zero. Therefore f(η)=∫0η​f′(s)ds≥ηf′(η), and the velocity formula gives 2ηf′−3f<0 for η>0. Consequently the transverse velocity is negative throughout that physical layer, and zero at the wall. This pointwise conclusion uses the positive decaying branch; the flux argument already establishes entrainment of the exterior.

Linearized mass conservation, momentum balance and the isentropic pressure-density relation are ρt′​+ρ0​∇⋅u=0, ρ0​ut​=−∇p​, and p​=c02​ρ′. Differentiate mass conservation in time and take the divergence of momentum balance to eliminate velocity. This gives the acoustic pressure wave equation
p​tt​=c02​∇2p​​.
(148)
For the convention p​=Reei(k⋅r−ωt), momentum balance gives the complex velocity amplitude k/(ρ0​ω), with ω=c0​∣k∣. Thus the incident velocity field is Re[kI​ei(kI​⋅r−ωt)/(ρ1​ω)] in the lower gas.
Let a=kI​sinθ, l1​=kI​cosθ>0, ω=c1​kI​, and l2​=(ω/c2​)2−a2​ with nonnegative real or imaginary part. This chooses an outgoing propagating wave or an evanescent wave decaying as y→+∞. Conservation of tangential wavevector is the acoustic Snell law for elastic and acoustic waves. Write the complex pressures as
p1​=ei(ax−ωt)(eil1​y+Re−il1​y),p2​=Tei(ax+l2​y−ωt).
(149)
Inviscid kinematic matching requires equal normal velocities at the plate, not equal tangential velocities:
ρ1​ωl1​​(1−R)=ρ2​ωl2​​T=−iωη0​.
(150)
Define the normal acoustic impedance ratio δ=ρ2​l1​/(ρ1​l2​), so T=δ(1−R). For a propagating transmitted wave this is ρ2​c2​cosθ/(ρ1​c1​cosθ2​). The dynamic condition gives
T−1−R=(mω2−Ba4)η0​=iβ(1−R),β=ρ1​ω2(mω2−Ba4)l1​​,
(151)
which is exactly the printed dimensionless parameter. Solving yields the pressure reflection coefficient and transmission coefficient
R=δ+1−iβδ−1−iβ​,T=δ+1−iβ2δ​​.
(152)
At l2​=0 use the preceding velocity equations, or take their limit, rather than substituting an infinite δ. For real l2​>0, the reflected energy fraction is ∣R∣2, the transmitted fraction is ∣T∣2/δ, and these sum to one. An evanescent transmitted wave carries no mean normal energy flux.
When the gases match, δ=1, so R=−iβ/(2−iβ) and T=2/(2−iβ). For a nongrazing incident wave of nonzero frequency, perfect transmission means R=0, equivalent to
β=0⟺mω2=BkI4​sin4θ⟺mc02​=BkI2​sin4θ​.
(153)
The plate's inertial and bending terms cancel: the incident frequency and tangential wavevector coincide with its free flexural wave dispersion relation. Then T=1, including its phase. With positive m,B, this condition is possible only at angles and frequencies satisfying that relation; for normal incidence at nonzero frequency it cannot occur unless the mass is zero.

ii OurBigBook.com
Away from a transmitted grazing or critical angle, ρ1​c1​≫ρ2​c2​ gives a small normal acoustic impedance ratio δ. Thus
R≃1−iβ−1−iβ​,∣R∣≃1​.
(154)
The reflected energy is nearly all the incident energy, while the pressure phase depends on the plate response. Large ∣β∣ gives R≃+1, resembling a rigid boundary; β≃0 gives R≃−1, resembling a pressure-release boundary. Bulk impedance contrast alone does not ensure δ≪1 arbitrarily close to a transmitted critical angle, since the factor 1/cosθ2​ can be large.
For fixed frequency and finite plate parameters, β contains the incident normal wavevector and therefore tends to zero as θ→π/2. If c1​=c2​, the outgoing l2​ tends to a nonzero real or imaginary value, whereas l1​→0, so δ→0 too. Consequently
R⟶−1(θ→π/2, c1​=c2​)​.
(155)
The lower-side boundary pressure 1+R tends to zero, regardless of how large the fixed m,B are. The angle must become closer to grazing as those parameters grow; the assertion is not uniform in an unbounded plate mass or rigidity.
If c1​=c2​, however, l2​=l1​ and δ=ρ2​/ρ1​ remains constant. The exact grazing limit is (δ−1)/(δ+1), rather than exactly −1 for finite contrast. Under the stated large-contrast approximation it is still arbitrarily close to the pressure-release value, with boundary pressure 2δ/(1+δ). Thus the printed pressure-release description is an approximation in that equal-speed case, not an exact zero-pressure identity. If a transmitted wave becomes evanescent, the outgoing square-root convention above continues to give the unequal-speed grazing limit.

39A OurBigBook.com
The Householder-John theorem states that if A=M−N is Hermitian positive definite and M∗+N is also Hermitian positive definite, then M is invertible and ρ(M−1N)<1. The associated stationary iteration x(k+1)=M−1Nx(k)+M−1b therefore converges from every starting vector. For designing a method, choose a splitting with easily solved M and verify the positive-definiteness condition on M∗+N; it is a sufficient certificate and does not require computing every iteration-matrix eigenvalue.
For completeness, put C=M∗+N=M∗+M−A. If Mv=0 for v=0, then v∗Cv=−v∗Av<0, a contradiction. If M−1Nv=zv, then Av=(1−z)Mv. The case z=1 contradicts invertibility of A. Taking scalar products and using Hermitian symmetry gives
(1−∣z∣2)v∗Av=∣1−z∣2v∗Cv>0,
(156)
hence ∣z∣<1. The usual spectral-radius convergence criterion now proves the stated conclusion.
For the given scheme take the matrix splitting
M=D/ω+L,N=(1/ω−1)D−U.
(157)
Since A is real symmetric, U=LT, and since it is positive definite, every diagonal entry in D is positive. Thus
MT+N=(2/ω−1)D
(158)
is positive definite exactly for 0<ω<2. The theorem applies, and the iteration matrix has spectral radius below one. The unique solution x∗​=A−1b is its fixed point, so x(k)−x∗​=(M−1N)k(x(0)−x∗​)→0. Therefore
x(k)→A−1bfor every x(0) and 0<ω<2​.
(159)
The scheme is successive over-relaxation; at ω=1 it becomes the Gauss-Seidel method.
